_: EP 11 — PagedAttention / vLLM. THE TRAVELLED-CANVAS EPISODE: there is one world (a memory map) and the camera lives inside it for the whole film. Beats are camera positions with annotation layers, not screens that replace each other — which is why nearly every `enter` is a cut. The two accents (flash on the title, dip-black into the honest limitation) are the only two moments continuity deliberately breaks. Every figure is sourced in references/ep11-facts.md; nothing here is remembered or rounded for effect. Display + technical face is Geist / Geist Mono, chosen against IBM Plex, Space Grotesk and Poppins on a rendered specimen — the metrics-matched pair matters because almost every beat sets a headline directly against a number.
title: Your chatbot doesn't stutter because of a trick from 1962.
subtitle: Eight hundred kilobytes a token, most of it thrown away, and an operating-system idea older than the GPU
hook: “A GPU runs out of memory long before it runs out of maths.”
next: Next: the regular expression that broke the internet
_voice: Series voice, unchanged from EP10: eleven_multilingual_v2, which CANNOT perform audio tags, so 'directive and unmodulated' is structural rather than a setting that drifts. House settings — stability 0.72, style 0.05. The authority is in the writing: imperatives, second person, front-loaded subjects, and a full stop where a weaker script would use a comma.
_music: 84 bpm, DECLARED not detected — we generate the bed ourselves, so the grid is exact by construction (the synth pads detect at only 0.6 confidence, correctly). `volume` is the ducked level under narration; `open` is where the bed sits when nobody is speaking. Beats 2 and 11 carry no VO on purpose: those are where the score gets to be music.
_vo: 12 spoken lines across 14 beats. Beat 2 (title) and beat 11 (the re-pack) are SILENT by design — the signature move earns a held silence with one thunk under it, and the bed lifts a full 7dB in both. Every figure is spelled as words, never digits. Eight of twelve lines are directive (second person or an instruction verb up front).

vo.text:
Watch a graphics card serve a language model.
It is not thinking. Most of the time… it is waiting.

Here is what nobody tells you.
A GPU runs out of MEMORY… long before it runs out of maths.
Every token you generate leaves keys and values behind. On a thirteen billion parameter model… eight hundred kilobytes each.

Look at the card.
Twenty six gigabytes… is the model itself.
Thirty percent is all the cache gets.
Now watch that disappear. Reserved space. Rounding up to the longest answer. Gaps. Only a third holds real tokens.

This is paging.
Cut the cache into fixed blocks.
Keep a table that says where each block really lives.
Two answers to one prompt share their blocks until they differ. Copy on write. Fifty five percent saved.

Count the result.
Two to four times the throughput of the best serving systems… Half the graphics cards.
Do not oversell this. Paging buys you memory, not intelligence. The model is no smarter… only cheaper to serve.
Memory was the bottleneck. Nineteen sixty two already had the answer. Next: the regular expression that broke the internet.

_shots: Five jobs. A travelled-canvas episode carries itself on the world, so this is well under the usual ten to twenty: one cold open, TWO theme elements (the surfaces the graphics sit on, one per value act), one saturated payoff, one close. A sixth job — the morph bridge into the world — is generated later from rendered Remotion stills, once there are frames to bridge between.
